title: Malaysia Airlines Flight 370
one_line: MH370 disappeared after leaving its route; its final location in the southern Indian Ocean remains unknown.
status_why: Radar, satellite data, and confirmed debris provide clues, but the main wreckage and cause remain unknown.

aircraft.livery_notes: White upper fuselage and tail; grey lower fuselage and nacelles; red and dark blue fuselage stripes; red and blue wau logo on tail. Visual reference is the cited 9M-MRO photograph published in March 2014. Its capture date is unknown; the older Visit Malaysia Year decal in that image is not verified for the accident date.

people.notes: All aboard are presumed dead; these are the official presumed-loss figures, not a count of recovered remains.

route.notes: Filed waypoints from Table 2.2B, printed p.295; DMS-style degrees/minutes converted arithmetically to decimal degrees. Departure clearance later replaced the SID with direct IGARI. The filed route is not the observed post-diversion path. Destination airport coordinates are a modern approximate reference point.

site.description: The evidence supports loss in the southern Indian Ocean, but there is no confirmed impact or seabed location. Search centres and seventh-arc vertices must not be displayed as the crash site.

environment.notes: Section 1.7, pp.96–101. MTSAT image at 17:32 showed no significant cloud at the last civil radar point; no cloud types, bases or tops are quantified. No lightning detected there during 16:00–21:59 UTC. Upper-air observations at Kota Bharu at 12:00 UTC 7 March and 00:00 UTC 8 March gave about -40 C and northeast wind at most 15 kt at 36,000 ft; these are nearby station profiles, not actual aircraft conditions. Surface METARs at four airports reported no significant phenomena, but numeric visibility and cloud layers are not reproduced in the report.

events.title: Airways clearance requested
events.detail: The first officer requested the airways clearance for Beijing. Ground radio recordings, rather than a recovered CVR, preserve this exchange.
events.caption: The first officer requested clearance for the flight to Beijing.

events.title: Pushback and start requested
events.detail: The crew requested pushback and engine start. No distress was reported.
events.caption: The crew requested permission to push back and start the engines. No distress was reported.

events.title: Cleared for takeoff
events.detail: Lumpur Tower cleared MH370 for takeoff.
events.caption: The tower cleared MH370 for takeoff.

events.title: Departure recorded
events.detail: The departure message records 16:42 UTC from Kuala Lumpur. The original ACARS series starts at 16:41:43; a precise wheels-off instant is not established here.
events.caption: MH370 departed Kuala Lumpur at about 16:42 UTC. The exact takeoff time isn't known.

events.title: Cleared direct to IGARI
events.detail: Departure cleared the aircraft to FL180 and replaced the SID with direct IGARI. This was an assigned flight level, not a recorded instantaneous altitude.
events.caption: Controllers cleared the aircraft to fly directly to IGARI and climb toward its assigned height.

events.title: Cleared to flight level 250
events.detail: The aircraft received clearance to climb to FL250.
events.caption: Controllers cleared the aircraft to climb higher.

events.title: Cleared to flight level 350
events.detail: The aircraft received clearance to climb to FL350.
events.caption: Controllers cleared the aircraft to climb to its cruising height.

events.title: Crew reported cruise level
events.detail: The crew reported maintaining FL350. The later ACARS batch contains pressure-altitude samples near that level.
events.caption: The crew reported reaching cruising height; automatic data also showed the aircraft near that level.

events.title: Last ACARS batch sent
events.detail: The last position batch contained six five-minute samples ending at 17:06:43. The last sample recorded 43,800 kg of fuel; it is not the fuel quantity at the transmission instant.
events.caption: The last automatic position message was sent, containing six earlier positions.

events.title: Cruise level reported again
events.detail: The crew again reported maintaining FL350. No problem was announced.
events.caption: The crew again reported flying at cruising height. No problem was announced.

events.title: Handover to Ho Chi Minh
events.detail: Lumpur Radar instructed MH370 to contact Ho Chi Minh on 120.9 MHz. No subsequent contact with that centre was established.
events.caption: Controllers instructed MH370 to contact Ho Chi Minh control, but no contact with that center followed.

events.title: Last recorded radio acknowledgement
events.detail: The captain acknowledged the handover. This quote is from the official report’s reproduction of ground-recorded radio traffic; no cockpit recording has been recovered.
events.quote: Good night Malaysian Three Seven Zero
events.locator: Section 1.1.1 p.2; voice attribution section 1.5.12 p.38
events.caption: The captain acknowledged the handover in the last recorded radio reply.

events.title: Last decoded Kota Bharu reply
events.detail: Independent decoding identifies the last Kota Bharu SSR reply at this time. It distinguishes received replies from the later disappearance of a coasted target on a display.
events.caption: The aircraft sent its last radar reply to Kota Bharu; its symbol remained on screens afterward.

events.title: Aircraft reached IGARI area
events.detail: The official radar chronology says the aircraft passed IGARI. A timed passage near a waypoint does not make the waypoint an exact radar coordinate.
events.caption: The aircraft passed near IGARI.

events.title: Last decoded ADS-B report
events.detail: The 2026 dataset ends ADS-B at about 6.93192 N, 103.59251 E. The final two messages omit the flight-level field; the data do not record a plunge to zero altitude.
events.locator: KT_ADSB_MH370.csv last row; CAPTION report pp.31,39–40

events.title: Mode S symbol disappeared
events.detail: The official chronology records loss of the Mode S display symbol at this time. Display timing differs from the individual reply times decoded later.
events.caption: One of the aircraft's radar symbols disappeared from controllers' screens.

events.title: Secondary radar symbol disappeared
events.detail: The final KL secondary-radar position symbol disappeared. Military radar subsequently traced the turnback; this display timestamp is not an exact timestamp for the transponder switch position.
events.caption: The aircraft's final position symbol disappeared from Kuala Lumpur radar. Military radar later tracked its turnback.

events.title: Primary return near Kota Bharu
events.detail: A primary radar return associated with the returning aircraft appears in the independently decoded Kota Bharu log. It supplies position, not a trustworthy altitude.
events.caption: Radar detected the returning aircraft near Kota Bharu, but did not reliably establish its height.

events.title: Controllers queried missing contact
events.detail: Ho Chi Minh queried Kuala Lumpur about MH370. A later table in the same report gives 17:39:03; the three-second discrepancy is retained in conflicts.
events.locator: Section 1.1.2 p.3; compare chronology in section 2.2
events.caption: Ho Chi Minh controllers asked Kuala Lumpur about the missing contact with MH370.

events.title: Phone registered near Penang
events.detail: A mobile network recorded a hit from the first officer’s phone at Bandar Baru Farlim. No call or message was recorded, and subsequent tests did not establish the aircraft’s altitude from this hit.
events.locator: Section 1.1.5 p.20; original time 01:52:27 MYT converted by subtracting eight hours
events.caption: The first officer's phone registered near Penang. No call or message was recorded.

events.title: Airline message failed to arrive

events.caption: The airline repeatedly sent messages asking the crew to contact Ho Chi Minh. The aircraft never acknowledged them.

events.title: Last military radar return
events.detail: The official report places the last military radar return about 10 nautical miles beyond MEKAR. Published map coordinates differ between sources, and no later unique aircraft position is recorded.
events.locator: Section 1.1.3 pp.4–5; Geoscience Australia radar geometry; UGIB Fig.3 p.4
events.caption: Military radar last detected the aircraft beyond MEKAR. No later exact position was recorded.

events.title: Satellite terminal logged on
events.detail: The aircraft terminal initiated a log-on, ending the satellite-link outage. A power interruption is the leading official explanation; its cause is unknown.
events.locator: Signalling Unit Log p.39; report conclusion p.441
events.caption: The aircraft reconnected to the satellite network, probably after a power interruption. The cause is unknown.

events.title: First satellite call went unanswered
events.detail: The ground station began call setup. The aircraft terminal exchanged signalling but the call was not answered.
events.locator: Signalling Unit Log p.40 and appendix 1
events.caption: The aircraft's satellite equipment responded to an incoming call, but the call went unanswered.

events.title: Satellite handshake 2
events.detail: The terminal responded with BTO 11500 microseconds and BFO 111 Hz. This constrains an arc, not a unique position.
events.caption: The aircraft answered a satellite check. The data narrowed its possible location to a curve.

events.title: Satellite handshake 3
events.detail: The terminal responded with BTO 11740 microseconds and BFO 141 Hz. This constrains an arc, not a unique position.
events.caption: Another satellite reply narrowed the aircraft's possible location to a curve, without identifying an exact position.

events.title: Rescue coordination centre activated
events.detail: Kuala Lumpur’s rescue coordination centre was activated after the prolonged loss of contact. The investigation criticised delays in alerting and coordination.
events.caption: Kuala Lumpur activated its rescue coordination center after a prolonged loss of contact.

events.title: Satellite handshake 4
events.detail: The terminal responded with BTO 12780 microseconds and BFO 168 Hz. This constrains an arc, not a unique position.
events.caption: The aircraft answered another satellite check, narrowing its possible location without giving an exact position.

events.title: Distress phase declared

events.title: Satellite handshake 5
events.detail: The terminal responded with BTO 14540 microseconds and BFO 204 Hz. This constrains an arc, not a unique position.
events.caption: Another satellite reply narrowed the aircraft's possible location to a curve, without identifying an exact position.

events.title: Second satellite call went unanswered

events.caption: A second satellite call went unanswered, although the aircraft's equipment responded.

events.title: Sixth arc response received

events.caption: The aircraft responded to a sixth satellite check, providing further satellite timing and frequency data.

events.title: Final log-on request received

events.locator: Signalling Unit Log p.41; Ashton Table 6
events.caption: The aircraft's satellite equipment requested another connection to the network.

events.caption: The final aircraft transmission suggested a rapid descent, but did not establish when or where impact occurred.

perspectives.label: Cause undetermined
perspectives.held_by: Malaysian ICAO Annex 13 Safety Investigation Team
perspectives.claim: The flight diverted and the initial turnback probably involved manual input. The investigation could not determine the cause, controller identity or motive, and did not establish a specific crash site.

evidence_for.text: Civil and military radar show the diversion, while satellite logs and identified debris support a southern Indian Ocean loss.
Simulator trials found manual control the likely way to reproduce the initial turnback.

evidence_against.text: Without wreckage, FDR and CVR, investigators could not rule out every technical failure or third-party intervention. The absence of a cause finding is a limit of evidence, not evidence for a particular conspiracy.

ending.description: Final location and instant remain unknown. The seventh arc constrains last transmissions, not the exact impact.

perspectives.label: Unresponsive flight and fuel exhaustion
perspectives.held_by: ATSB search strategy working group, with Boeing, Inmarsat and DST Group
perspectives.claim: The search used an extended, largely stable southern flight ending near fuel exhaustion as its leading working scenario. A final loss and restoration of electrical power could explain the terminal log-on; this does not prove why the crew were unresponsive or when that began.

evidence_for.text: Long flight without normal communications, fuel modelling, and the final log-on support exhaustion of engine fuel and a brief APU-powered restart.
Holland’s calibrated final BFO analysis supports a rapidly increasing descent. Debris examination favoured a retracted right outboard flap at separation.

evidence_against.text: Pilot consciousness and controls were not recorded after the early flight. Missing wreckage leaves impact location, a possible recovery from descent, and the exact end scenario unresolved.
The main wreckage was not found in the large searched regions. This constrains those regions but does not, by itself, determine a different cause.

ending.description: An unpiloted descent after fuel exhaustion near the seventh arc is favoured for search design; no unique impact coordinate or rate is asserted.

perspectives.label: Inmarsat illustrative path
perspectives.claim: The paper gives one path consistent with much of the timing and frequency evidence. The authors explicitly say many other routes fit and that its endpoint is uncertain.

evidence_for.text: The example matches five late signalling BFO samples within about 2 Hz.

evidence_against.text: Its assumptions and rounded samples do not identify the real route. The final BFO differs greatly from a level-flight prediction and requires a separate end-of-flight interpretation.

ending.description: Example last-contact position, not a measured crash location or a new recommended search hotspot.

perspectives.label: UGIB due-south route
perspectives.held_by: Bobby Ulich, Richard Godfrey, Victor Iannello and Andrew Banks, 2020; later Ulich and Iannello drift work
perspectives.claim: UGIB combines satellite data, aircraft performance, weather, fuel and drift evidence to favour a due-south late route. It proposes a low-altitude segment before the final southbound cruise; that detailed early path and claims of planned diversion are not official findings.

evidence_for.text: Its constrained route and fuel model give a last estimated position at 34.2342 S, 93.7875 E. The 2023 drift work favours a nearby latitude, with much broader uncertainty.
The authors identify steep terrain and incomplete earlier sonar coverage as reasons for checking some already surveyed regions again.

evidence_against.text: The preferred point depends on navigation mode, airspeed/fuel settings, timing corrections, assumed altitude and limited later pilot input; fitting those assumptions is not unique proof of the route.
The 2025–2026 contracted search still reported no confirmed wreckage, and exact AUV coverage relative to every proposed subzone is not public in the sources used.

ending.description: Conditional last estimated position; UGIB section 8.2 assumes 20,000 ft geometric height for this arc crossing. Later glide and descent uncertainty prevent treating it as an exact impact point.

perspectives.label: CSIRO drift region
perspectives.held_by: CSIRO oceanographers David Griffin, Peter Oke and collaborators
perspectives.claim: CSIRO drift work favoured a region near 35 S, within a broader southern section of the seventh arc. Part III proposed a tighter location only if certain unconfirmed objects in satellite imagery were MH370 debris.

evidence_for.text: Measured drift characteristics of a damaged genuine flaperon made the Réunion arrival timing easier to explain. Other finds and non-detections constrained the likely origin; Part IV revisited the limits of the surface-search exclusion.
Part III’s conditional back-drift analysis nominated 35.6 S, 92.8 E and nearby alternatives.

evidence_against.text: The image objects were never recovered or identified as MH370. Find dates may lag beaching dates, and long drift modelling has uncertainty.
A predicted source region is not a discovered wreckage site; later searches have not confirmed it.

ending.description: Conditional debris-origin hypothesis from CSIRO Part III, not a measured last aircraft position. No invented flight path or crash time.

perspectives.label: Controlled final descent
perspectives.held_by: Larry Vance; Vincent Lyne’s 2024 paper; some independent analysts
perspectives.claim: This view allows pilot control near the end, potentially a glide or controlled water entry farther from the seventh arc. Lyne argues that a coupled-motion model favours an eastward descent; it is a reinterpretation of the final signals, not evidence of an identified pilot action.

evidence_for.text: The final BFOs are indirect measurements with oscillator and flight-motion modelling assumptions, and the recovered trailing-edge damage has been interpreted differently.
Ulich and Iannello’s search recommendations also explicitly allow for a substantial glide, without establishing that it occurred.

evidence_against.text: Official examination found the right outboard flap most likely retracted, weakening a conventional flaps-extended ditching interpretation.
Holland’s analysis already varies track, speed, oscillator startup and noise; it still supports rapid descent. Neither interpretation establishes a subsequent recovery or controlled impact.

ending.description: Possible continued glide or eastward movement after final contact; location, control inputs, recovery and impact time unknown. No unsupported exact trajectory supplied.

perspectives.label: WSPR tracking claim
perspectives.held_by: Richard Godfrey and WSPR-method collaborators; opposed by Iannello, Ulich, Exner and other critics
perspectives.claim: Godfrey attributes anomalies in amateur-radio propagation reports to MH370 and infers a detailed route and later endpoint. Those reports do not directly identify an aircraft; this contested inference is excluded from the observed replay.

evidence_for.text: The proponent reports multiple signal anomalies and asserts consistency with satellite constraints and case studies. This is his claimed support, not independently verified MH370 detection.

evidence_against.text: Iannello’s link-budget analysis finds aircraft-scattered signals too weak at the relevant distances and notes that ionospheric propagation itself produces variability.
The WSPR database lacks the full signal information needed to isolate aircraft Doppler scattering, and no physical debris field verifies the claimed endpoint.

ending.description: Proponent’s February 2024 model endpoint. The time and location are not observations; no per-minute WSPR route was copied without checking its complete source table.

perspectives.label: Technical emergency and incapacitation
perspectives.held_by: Technical-failure or hypoxia scenario proponents; considered but unproven by the Malaysian investigation
perspectives.claim: A technical emergency followed by incapacitation could explain unanswered communications and an extended autopilot flight. The official investigation did not find a failure sequence that explained all the observed deactivations and route changes, but could not exclude every technical possibility.

evidence_for.text: SATCOM outages and later restoration can result from power interruptions; long silent flight is compatible with incapacitation. These facts do not establish hypoxia, fire or the timing of either.

evidence_against.text: The diversion and several direction changes are difficult to attribute to anomalous systems alone. No recorded fault, distress call or verified fire evidence establishes this scenario.

ending.description: Continued autopilot flight until fuel exhaustion is possible, but the emergency’s nature, start time, cabin state and final path remain unknown.

perspectives.label: Java acoustic candidate
perspectives.held_by: Ed Anderson; Victor Iannello recommended a limited check in March 2026
perspectives.claim: Anderson links an acoustic/seismic event to a possible MH370 seabed impact near Java. Iannello recommends checking the small candidate area while explicitly stating that the sound cannot be definitively linked to MH370.

evidence_for.text: The proponent reports a localisable acoustic event near the seventh arc and argues it could be a sinking airframe’s seabed arrival.

evidence_against.text: An acoustic source location does not identify the source as MH370, and this location is well north of the leading performance and drift regions. No wreckage has confirmed the association.

ending.description: Candidate acoustic-source area; not an observed aircraft endpoint. Event-to-aircraft association and any preceding route remain unverified.

perspectives.label: Remote takeover claim
perspectives.held_by: Some public remote-control takeover proponents; rejected by Malaysian investigators
perspectives.claim: This claim invokes Boeing’s patented remote-takeover technology as a way the aircraft could have been flown from the ground. Investigators found no evidence the proposed technology had been installed or used on 9M-MRO.

evidence_for.text: A Boeing patent existed; a patent is not evidence of installation on this aircraft.

evidence_against.text: Boeing and the operator confirmed the patented system had not been installed, and the investigation found no supporting evidence.

ending.description: No evidenced alternative route or endpoint. A patent does not justify adding remote-control actions to the replay.

conflicts.about: ACARS typed table versus reproduced original message
conflicts.b: Figure 1.9H p.114 shows the original message: 2.767, 101.988, 102.534 and 102.813 respectively. conflicts.about: Last transmitted reply versus last displayed radar symbol
conflicts.a: The 2018 report records Mode S display loss at 17:20:36 and final secondary display loss at 17:21:13.
conflicts.b: CAPTION’s raw-data decoding identifies last KB SSR reply 17:20:30.656, Kuantan SSR reply 17:20:32.685, and ADS-B 17:20:34.555. Later display coasting and data processing need not mean the transponder remained transmitting to 17:21:13.

conflicts.a: The report reproduces returns ranging from 4,800 to 47,500 ft and extreme point-to-point speed/height changes.
conflicts.b: The same report warns the extracted military altitude and speed were inherently erroneous and beyond aircraft capability; only latitude/longitude were considered useful. Those heights and speeds are not used as observed 3D states.

conflicts.a: Geoscience Australia RADAR_Points OID277: about 6.5992 N, 96.31222 E; radar connector endpoint is slightly different again.
conflicts.b: UGIB 2020 Fig.3: about 6.578 N, 96.341 E at 18:22:12. The latter is not silently substituted for the government map point; map/generalisation and underlying source differences are unresolved.

conflicts.about: Time Ho Chi Minh queried Kuala Lumpur
conflicts.b: A later chronology table says 17:39:03 UTC. Both are retained; the brief does not claim sub-second certainty for this exchange.

conflicts.a: Inmarsat’s illustrative level-flight path places the aircraft on a southerly track by the call.
conflicts.b: UGIB permits a westward descent during the call, followed by a later major south turn. Vertical motion can alter BFO, so the call does not uniquely timestamp the south turn.

conflicts.about: Seventh-arc BTO correction and altitude convention
conflicts.a: Ashton Table 6 uses 23,000 minus 4,600 = 18,400 μs and initially excludes the final acknowledgement’s anomalous BTO.
conflicts.b: UGIB section 8.2 uses corrected 18,422 and 18,387 μs, combines them to 18,390 μs, and assumes 20,000 ft geometric height. These lead to slightly different arc positions; the raw logs are preserved separately.

conflicts.a: Official examination favours retracted right outboard flap and near-neutral flaperon at separation; Holland favours accelerating descent.
conflicts.b: Vance and Lyne favour controlled descent or water entry and a different interpretation of flap damage. No FDR, CVR or recovered main wreckage confirms pilot control or an exact impact sequence.

conflicts.a: Ashton’s example ends near 34.7 S, 93 E; UGIB’s constrained solution near 34.2342 S, 93.7875 E.
conflicts.b: CSIRO Part III conditionally favours 35.6 S, 92.8 E, whereas later Ulich/Iannello drift work peaks nearer 34 S with broader uncertainty. Different assumptions and uncertain evidence prevent one being treated as measured truth.

conflicts.a: Godfrey claims WSPR anomalies identify MH370 positions and an endpoint near 29.128 S, 99.934 E.
conflicts.b: Iannello and other critics argue the link budget and missing signal information prevent this identification and that ordinary propagation variability explains the claimed anomalies. No independent radar or wreckage confirmation resolves this in the proponent’s favour.

conflicts.a: The official 2026 update counts contracted phases from 25 March 2025 and 31 December 2025, with about 7,571 km² and 28 operational days.
conflicts.b: The same update acknowledges earlier unquantified survey work; ship-tracking accounts may count mobilisation or pre-contract operations. Ocean Infinity’s more than 140,000 km² is cumulative since 2018 and is not contradictory proof of a much larger 2026 contracted survey.

conflicts.a: Historical Malaysian AIP places WMKK’s ARP at 02°44′36″N 101°41′53″E with published elevation 70 ft.
conflicts.b: The modern airport dataset uses 2.74558 N, 101.709999 E and 69 ft. Those are airport reference conventions/database values, not the aircraft’s rotation position; the historical AIP is used for route.from.

unknowns: Main wreckage location, impact coordinate, water depth, impact UTC time and disposition of the aircraft. Government and operator sources through 2026 report no confirmed location.
FDR and CVR contents: neither recorder recovered. There are no actual final-minute FDR pitch, roll, angle-of-attack, engine or configuration tables to extract.

Why communications ceased, what caused the early satellite power interruption, who controlled the aircraft, whether any unlawful interference occurred, and motive. No allegation against an individual is established here.
Exact turnback path and altitude during the gap between last SSR/ADS-B and returning primary-radar coverage. Dense later plots do not fill this gap.

True altitude above mean sea level. Pressure altitude/flight levels and GNSS ellipsoid height are available before signal loss but not converted without a defensible datum and atmospheric model. alt_ft therefore stays null; source pressure and ellipsoid heights remain in explicit extra fields.
Reliable post-diversion altitude and military point-to-point speeds. The official report warns that these outputs are erroneous; independent proposed climbs and descents are hypotheses.
Exact point and time of the final south turn, navigation/autopilot modes, later manoeuvres and any post-00:19 recovery or glide. Satellite arcs alone do not specify these.

Exact wind, cloud types/bases/tops, visibility, turbulence, illumination, moon, sea state and wave height at impact. The location/time are not known, and nearby weather profiles cannot be substituted for an impact observation.
Exact wheels-off second. The official departure message gives 16:42 UTC and the ACARS sample starts at 16:41:43; these are distinct records.
A verified manufacturer numeric wing-sweep value in the primary material read. wing_sweep_deg is null; no value is guessed from a drawing.
Exact loss-date decorative livery decals. The inspected photograph establishes base colours, but its older Visit Malaysia Year marking is not dated to March 2014.

Exact authoritative seafloor search polygons and per-AUV actual coverage for Ocean Infinity’s 2018 and 2025–2026 operations. Published area totals and approximate overview extents do not establish scanned footprints; missing geometries remain null.
Exact authoritative 2025 contract polygon vertices. The 2024 proposal display corridor is an explicitly calculated approximation and cannot be substituted for the signed 15,000 km² area.

Whether operations actually resumed by 7 November 2026. June’s extension and November–April deployment window are verified in a visually inspected reproduction of the minister’s statement and contemporary news reporting, but no opened primary release confirms an actual November restart.
Exact UTC instants for shoreline recoveries, public report releases and contract-phase calendar dates. Source dates are retained without inventing midnight; find dates are not beaching dates.
Whether the unconfirmed Pleiades-image objects or the Java acoustic event were related to MH370. Neither is labelled an identified aircraft detection.

A defensible unique per-vertex time for Geoscience Australia’s military path geometry. The independent spreadsheet’s estimated times are explicitly unsuitable for calculating inter-point speeds, so those times were not used.

A verified complete time-position table for Godfrey’s WSPR route. Only the opened, attributed endpoint claim is retained as a minority hypothesis; its claimed 130 positions are not invented or promoted to radar.

date_notes: The familiar date, 8 March 2014, is Malaysian local time. Departure and the loss of radar contact occurred on 7 March UTC; the final satellite messages were on 8 March UTC. Report p.1 footnote defines MYT = UTC+08:00.
reconstruction_notes: No FDR or CVR has been recovered. No onboard cockpit audio is available. The brief contains only the official ground-recorded last radio acknowledgement as a quote.

Main track contains individual observed telemetry/radar records plus position-null satellite markers. It contains no interpolated samples. Unknown gaps must be visible, including the turnback gap and the long post-radar segment.

alt_ft is reserved for established feet MSL. Available FL/ACARS ALT values are retained in pressure_alt_ft; ADS-B geometric height in geometric_alt_ellipsoid_ft. Neither is silently relabelled MSL. A viewer may offer a clearly labelled nominal pressure-altitude view, but it cannot claim an exact 3D height.

hdg_deg has heading_reference when populated. Comm-B heading is magnetic; ACARS THDG is true. ground_track_deg is a separate direction of motion and must not be used as aircraft heading without a model.

Coordinates in GeoJSON geometry use [longitude, latitude], unlike the lat/lon objects elsewhere. Source vertices are retained, including their source precision; that precision is not a survey-accuracy claim.
No fabricated crash animation, end-of-flight pitch, bank, impact time, or final descent rate is supplied. Published alternatives are opt-in perspectives, not continuations of the observed track.

Date-only events have t_utc=null and calendar_date with the source’s calendar basis. No midnight UTC is invented. Aircraft samples and exact-time events are ordered; date-only events are placed in calendar order.
